summary:
Field Shift — Rotation Replay is a web tool developed by an Amman-based team to help rain-fed farmers in Jordan (specifically Irbid, Mafraq, and Madaba) mitigate the risks of unpredictable rainfall. Designed under human direction with AI assistance, the tool allows farmers to simulate and test crop rotation changes against historical climate data before committing to a real season.
Farmers locate their field on a map, input soil type, water supply, current rotation, and six specific farming priorities (like reliable harvests or animal feed). The tool then simulates both current and alternative rotations day-by-day using 40 years of localized NASA POWER weather data (1985–2025).
Instead of an uncertain future forecast, Field Shift delivers results as historical odds. It displays the current rotation alongside the three best alternative options, evaluating them based on:
• The percentage of historically "poor" seasons
• A year-by-year performance timeline
• A comprehensive water budget
• Plain-language notes outlining suggestions, evidence, gaps, and local checks
This tool addresses a critical vulnerability: in dry regions like Irbid, an average of only 68% of sown wheat was harvested between 1996 and 2006. While testing new rotations traditionally takes years in the field, this tool delivers data-driven viability insights in seconds, identifying where data cannot be trusted to prevent costly seasonal losses.
details:
The problem

About 90% of Jordan receives less than 200 mm of rain a year. Renewable water is about 61 m³ per person per year, and agriculture uses more than half of the country’s fresh water. Jordan grows roughly 3% of the wheat it eats.

Rain-fed cereal farming is concentrated in the wetter north and centre, and it is risky. In Irbid, on average only 68% of the wheat area and 44% of the barley area sown was harvested between 1996 and 2006. A 1988 survey around Mafraq found 45.5% of farmers growing barley after barley every year and 27% alternating barley with fallow; 83.6% owned sheep. Long-term trials in neighbouring Syria show the cost of these habits and the alternatives: continuous barley yields declined over time, a barley–vetch rotation produced 29% more total biomass, and wheat–lentil and wheat–vetch rotations produced 27% more grain per rotation than wheat–fallow.

A farmer cannot test such a change quickly. One trial of a two-year rotation takes two years and covers two kinds of weather. The long weather record that NASA publishes makes a different test possible: replay the last 40 years on the farmer’s own field.

What it does

  1. Pick the field. The farmer clicks a point on a map. Three demo fields in Jordan (Irbid, Mafraq, Madaba) load instantly. Any other point on Earth works and fetches its data live.
  2. Describe the farm. Current rotation (default: wheat then fallow), soil type (sandy, loam or clay), water supply (rain-fed or a seasonal irrigation budget), and the farmer’s own rain-gauge average if known.
  3. Set priorities. Six sliders: reliable harvests, use less water, build soil health, break pest cycles, income potential, animal feed.
    • the share of seasons that would have been poor (below 50% of the crop’s potential yield);
    • a year-by-year timeline of good and bad harvests;
    • the yield range in a typical, a bad and a good year;
    • a water budget: rain, water used by crops, evaporation from bare soil, runoff, and drainage below the roots;
    • five plain-language sections: Why it was suggested, Evidence, Benefits, Information gaps, Check locally.
  4. Ask “what if”. Two sliders change rainfall (−40% to +20%) and temperature (0 to +4 °C) and rerun the replay at once. This shows which rotation holds up in a drier, hotter climate.
  5. Look at the satellite record. A panel shows the field’s greenness curve from the MODIS satellite instrument (NDVI, defined below) and the periods when the field is bare. Map overlays show NASA imagery of vegetation, soil moisture, rainfall and land-surface temperature.

The tool is a static website. It has no backend and no accounts.

How it works

All calculations run in the browser, in TypeScript.

Weather. Daily maximum and minimum temperature and rainfall for 1985–2025 come from the NASA POWER service, which is based on NASA’s MERRA-2 reanalysis (a reconstruction of past weather on a grid of cells about 50 km wide).

Combining satellite-era data with ground measurements. A 50 km cell hides local differences, so the tool corrects two things:

  • Rainfall. NASA POWER supplies the daily sequence and the swings from year to year. The long-term average is rescaled to the farmer’s own rain-gauge average if given. Otherwise it is rescaled to the 1991–2020 average from CHIRPS, a 5 km rainfall dataset that blends satellite and station data, obtained through NASA SERVIR ClimateSERV. If neither is available, NASA POWER is used unchanged and the tool says so.
  • Temperature. Temperature is moved from the average elevation of the grid cell to the field’s own elevation (Copernicus DEM), at 6.5 °C per kilometre of height.

Water demand. Evapotranspiration is the water that leaves a field by evaporating from soil and passing through plants. Reference evapotranspiration is calculated each day with the Hargreaves–Samani equation (FAO-56 equation 52). A crop’s water demand is that value multiplied by a crop coefficient (Kc) that changes with growth stage, using the coefficients and stage lengths published in FAO-56.

Soil water. The soil is modelled as two layers, 0–0.15 m and 0.15–1.5 m, like two buckets. Each day rain enters, some runs off (SCS curve-number method), crops draw water from the depth their roots have reached, bare soil loses water from the top layer only, and any excess drains below the roots. When the soil dries past a crop-specific point, the crop’s water use is cut (the FAO-56 water-stress coefficient, Ks).

Yield. Relative yield is the share of a crop’s potential yield that it reaches. It is calculated as 1 − Ky × (1 − actual water use ÷ water demand), the FAO-33 yield-response equation, where Ky is a published factor for each crop. It is then reduced for temperatures outside the crop’s range, frost at flowering, heat at flowering, and by 15% when a crop follows another of the same plant family without a break.

Sowing. Seeds wait for rain. A sown crop only starts when the top layer holds at least 40% of its water capacity. If that does not happen within 75 days, the season is counted as lost. For each crop the tool searches the whole record for the sowing date that performs best. In Jordan this makes crops establish in November, which matches local crop calendars.

Rotations. A crop is treated as viable at a location if it averages at least 40% of its potential yield at its best sowing date. Every two-year and three-year rotation of the viable crops and bare fallow is generated; the same crop is never suggested two years running. Each rotation is simulated once for every starting phase, so every crop meets every year. An optional cover crop (a crop grown only to protect the soil between main crops) is kept only where it had enough warmth and water to grow.

Scoring. Each rotation gets six scores from 0 to 100, one per priority, and the farmer’s sliders weight them into one ranking. The three top-ranked rotations that differ from each other and from the current one are shown.

Crops. Fourteen crops: wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, faba bean, vetch, berseem clover, sorghum, pearl millet, maize, soybean, sunflower, canola and potato, plus bare fallow.

Satellite evidence. NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) is a satellite measure of how green the ground is. The tool reads the MODIS NDVI time series for the field’s pixel (250 m, every 16 days) to show the real growing season and bare periods. NASA GIBS map layers add context around the field.

Testing. The model code has 17 automated unit tests (Vitest).

What we checked, and what we found

  • Rainfall data against a ground station. We compared season rainfall with Irbid station seasons 1996–2006 published by Al-Bakri et al. (2010). NASA POWER followed the year-to-year swings well (correlation r ≈ 0.93), but its grid cell averaged only about 176 mm against the station’s 472 mm. CHIRPS was closer on average (about 350 mm) but flattened drought years: it put the 1999 drought at 86% of normal when stations recorded about 45%. This is why the tool takes the sequence from one source and the average from another, and why it asks the farmer for a rain-gauge average.
  • Crop calendar. With the correction, crops establish in November, as Jordanian crop calendars say.
  • Where crops fail. The model finds wheat viable at Irbid (472 mm) and not viable at Mafraq (160 mm), where barley is also poor in about 8 of 10 seasons. National statistics show that only 23–69% of Jordan’s barley area was harvested in 2007–2017.
  • A known drought. The model ranks the 1999 harvest among the worst. That year only 8% of Irbid’s wheat area was harvested.
  • A known rotation effect. The model shows wheat after fallow out-yielding continuous wheat. The ICARDA long-term trial at Tel Hadya, Syria, found the same direction. The real gap there was larger than ours (2.43 against 1.08 t/ha).

Limits

  • Results are a share of each crop’s potential yield, not tonnes per hectare.
  • Pests, diseases, soil fertility, crop varieties and prices are not modelled.
  • The soil is assumed uniform and 1.5 m deep. Shallow, stony or saline soils will do worse.
  • NASA POWER rainfall appears to have a spurious upward trend at this location, so the tool does not report rainfall trends.
  • Crop temperature thresholds, and the market and forage rankings, are approximate.
  • The suggested rotations have not been validated against field trials.
  • The replay is more optimistic than real farms. In Irbid about a third of the wheat area sown went unharvested in 1996–2006; the replay shows fewer poor seasons than that. The numbers are best read as a comparison between rotations, not as a forecast.
  • The one-station rainfall comparison covers eleven seasons at one site.

The tool supports farmer judgment and extension advice. It does not replace them. Every rotation card lists its information gaps and the points to review with a local extension office.

Benefits

  • A farmer or extension agent gets a first, field-specific answer in seconds instead of after several seasons.
  • The answer is given as risk (“33% of seasons poor, 13 of 39”), which is how a rain-fed farmer weighs a decision, not as a single average.
  • Each suggestion carries its reasons, evidence and gaps, so it can be questioned.
  • It costs nothing to run: open data, a static site, no server, no login.
  • It works for any point on Earth, because every input is global.

What we hope to achieve

  • A pilot with extension staff: Jordan’s National Agricultural Research Center (NARC) and Ministry of Agriculture directorates advise the country’s farms.
  • An Arabic interface.
  • A mid-season update: compare this autumn’s rain so far with the years in the record that started the same way, before the sowing decision. It needs a rainfall source that is current to within a few days, which we have not verified.
  • Real prices, so that income is shown in money. As a starting point, 2025 government purchase prices were 420 JOD per tonne for wheat and 370 JOD per tonne for barley.
  • Soil-test input in place of the uniform-soil assumption.
  • Comparison of the suggested rotations with field-trial results.

Tools, languages and software

  • TypeScript, React, Vite (web app); Leaflet (map); Vitest (unit tests); pnpm (packages).
  • GitHub Pages (hosting).
  • Data services called from the browser: NASA POWER API, ORNL DAAC MODIS subset API, NASA GIBS, NASA SERVIR ClimateSERV, Open-Meteo elevation API, OpenStreetMap tiles.
  • Claude (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant. See the next section.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

We used an AI coding assistant, Claude by Anthropic.

  • Code. Most of the application code, the crop parameter table, the unit tests and the data-fetching scripts were generated with Claude. Source files that were AI-generated say so in a comment at the top.
  • Text. The README and the slides design were done with Claude.
  • Research. Claude was used to find and summarise some published sources listed below, and to run the validation comparisons described above.
  • The team’s part. The team chose the challenge, the direction of the project and the demo region, gave the instructions, and reviewed the output, also wrote the main code, sorted out the linked in the web page and tested the app.
  • Images. The project contains no AI-generated images, video or audio. All images are screenshots of the running tool or simple diagrams drawn in code.
  • In the product. The tool itself does not use an AI or machine-learning model. Its results come from a published water-balance method (FAO-56 and FAO-33) that can be checked step by step.

No NASA logos, flags, mission patches or branding are used.

NASA Data

Product

Provider

How we use it

NASA POWER daily API, Agroclimatology community (based on MERRA-2). Parameters: T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, GWETROOT; 1985–2025

NASA Langley Research Center, POWER project

The core input. Daily maximum and minimum temperature and rainfall drive the day-by-day replay of every rotation. Root-zone soil wetness (GWETROOT) is shown as climate context.

MODIS MOD13Q1 vegetation index (NDVI), 250 m, 16-day

ORNL DAAC MODIS/VIIRS subset API

A time series for the field’s pixel shows the real greenness curve and the periods when the field is bare. It is evidence beside the model, not an input to it.

NASA GIBS map layers: MODIS NDVI, SMAP Level-4 root-zone soil moisture, GPM IMERG precipitation, MODIS land-surface temperature

NASA Global Imagery Browse Services (WMTS)

Map overlays that let the farmer see vegetation, soil moisture, rainfall and surface temperature around the field.

CHIRPS rainfall through ClimateSERV

NASA SERVIR (data by the UCSB Climate Hazards Center and USGS)

The 1991–2020 mean annual rainfall at about 5 km. Used to correct the long-term rainfall average of the NASA POWER grid cell when the farmer has no rain gauge.

Methods

  • Allen, R.G., Pereira, L.S., Raes, D., Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration: guidelines for computing crop water requirements. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56. (Reference evapotranspiration, crop coefficients, stage lengths, water-stress coefficient.)
  • Doorenbos, J., Kassam, A.H. (1979). Yield response to water. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33. (Yield-response factors.)
  • FAO ECOCROP database. (Crop temperature ranges, rounded.)
  • USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Technical Release 55. (SCS runoff curve numbers.)

Papers and reports

  • Al-Bakri et al. (2010). Physics and Chemistry of the Earth. doi:10.1016/j.pce.2010.06.001 — Irbid station rainfall and harvested-area shares, 1996–2006.
  • Ryan et al. (2010). Journal of Agricultural Science. doi:10.1017/S0021859609990566 — ICARDA Tel Hadya long-term rotation trial.
  • Jones & Singh (2000). Journal of Agricultural Science. doi:10.1017/S0021859699008205 — barley rotations, 14-year trials in Syria.
  • Pala et al. (2007). ICARDA. https://repo.mel.cgiar.org/handle/20.500.11766/11992 — wheat-based rotations compared with wheat–fallow.
  • Oglah & Jaradat (1988). Survey of barley farmers around Mafraq. https://agris.fao.org/search/en/records/6471c74a77fd37171a6f1b3e
  • UNW-DPC (2014). Jordan drought country report. https://www.droughtmanagement.info/literature/UNW-DPC_NDMP_Country_Report_Jordan_2014.pdf — rainfall distribution and station means.
  • US International Trade Administration. Jordan country commercial guide, environment and water sector. https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/jordan-environment-and-water-sector — water per person, agricultural share.
  • USDA Foreign Agricultural Service. Report JO2026-0002 — Jordan wheat production and consumption.
  • Jordan News (2025). Ministry of Agriculture purchase prices for local wheat and barley. https://www.jordannews.jo/Section-109/News/Ministry-of-Agriculture-Collection-of-Local-Wheat-and-Barley-Crops-Begins-43407
  • ICARDA and NARC (2020), barley sector report for Jordan, Table 1: national barley area cultivated and harvested 2007–2017 (harvested share 23–69%, our arithmetic from the table). https://mel.cgiar.org/reporting/downloadmelspace/hash/10dde90806547784709f03b7e922e9dc/v/dc517e9ebb1ea37ae5e5484073078e90
